# Research Question:

# Dependent & Independent Variables:

Dependent Variable: price

Independent Variable 1 (Continuous): sqft_living

Independent Variable 2 (Categorical): waterfront

Independent Variable 3 (Discrete?): bedrooms

# Data Preparation

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(modelr)

house_sales <- read.csv("kc_house_data.csv")

house_sales$waterfront <- factor(house_sales$waterfront)

str(house_sales)
```

# Model 1 - Parallel-Lines Model (sqft_living, waterfront, and bedrooms)

$$
\text{price}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{sqft\_living}_i + \beta_2\,\text{waterfront}_i + \beta_3\,\text{bedrooms}_i + \varepsilon_i
$$

```{r}
model1 <- lm(price ~ sqft_living + waterfront + bedrooms, data = house_sales)
summary(model1)
```

## Visualization

```{r}
grid_parallel <- expand.grid(
  sqft_living = seq(min(house_sales$sqft_living), max(house_sales$sqft_living), length.out = 50),
  waterfront  = levels(house_sales$waterfront),
  bedrooms    = median(house_sales$bedrooms)
)
grid_parallel$price_pred <- predict(model1, newdata = grid_parallel)
```

```{r}
ggplot(house_sales, aes(x = sqft_living, y = price, color = waterfront)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = grid_parallel, aes(y = price_pred, color = waterfront), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = paste0("Parallel Lines Model (bedrooms held at ", median(house_sales$bedrooms), ")"),
       x = "sqft_living", y = "price") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r, fig.height = 4}
# (2) one panel per bedroom count (2, 3, 4 bedrooms)
bed_values <- unique(house_sales$bedrooms)

grid_bed <- expand.grid(
  sqft_living = seq(min(house_sales$sqft_living), max(house_sales$sqft_living), length.out = 50),
  waterfront  = levels(house_sales$waterfront),
  bedrooms    = bed_values
)
grid_bed$price_pred <- predict(model1, newdata = grid_bed)

ggplot(filter(house_sales, bedrooms %in% bed_values),
       aes(x = sqft_living, y = price, color = waterfront)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = grid_bed, aes(y = price_pred), linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ bedrooms, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(title = "Parallel Lines Model by Number of Bedrooms",
       x = "sqft_living", y = "price") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Diagnostics

### Mean Zero and Homoscedasticity

#### Residuals vs Fitted plot

```{r}
# Residuals vs Fitted
plot(model1, which = 1)
```

Based on the Residuals vs. Fitted graph, it seems that the assumption of Mean zero-errors is generally fulfilled, as the red line is centered generally at zero, except at the far ends of the graph where there's very few data points and potential outliers.

#### Scale-Location plot

```{r}
# Scale-Location plot
plot(model1, which = 3)
```

The Scale-Location graph, along with the Residuals vs. Fitted Graph, suggests that the variance is not constant across X, as we see an upward trend in the Scale-Location plot. In other words, our data does not fulfill the assumption of homoscedasticity.

### Normality

```{r}
model1_withres <- house_sales %>% 
  add_residuals(model1)
qqnorm(model1_withres$resid, main = "Normal Q–Q Plot")
qqline(model1_withres$resid, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```

```{r}
hist(model1_withres$resid, prob = TRUE, breaks = 50, col = "lightcoral",
main = "Residual Histogram", xlab = "Residuals")
grid <- sort(model1_withres$resid)
lines(grid, dnorm(grid, mean = mean(model1_withres$resid),
sd = sd(model1_withres$resid)),
col = "maroon", lwd = 2)
```

Given the Q-Q Plot and residual histogram, it seems that the points does not follow the diagonal line or the normal distribution closely, suggesting that the assumption of normality is not fulfilled.

### Outliers

```{r}
plot(model1, which = 4)
```

```{r}
plot(model1, which = 5)
```

## Testing & Confidence Interval

### Summary

```{r}
aggregate(price ~ bedrooms, data = house_sales, FUN = mean)
```

### Visualization

```{r}
house_sales$bedrooms <- factor(house_sales$bedrooms)
ggplot(house_sales,
       aes(x = bedrooms, y = price, fill = bedrooms)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6) +
  ggtitle("Price by Bedrooms") +
  xlab("# of Bedrooms") +
  ylab("Price") + 
  theme_minimal()
```
### ANOVA

```{r}
anova(model1)
```
While the ANOVA has significantly low p-values for all coefficients, the diagnostics earlier tell us that assumptions for the test are not met, so other, non-parametric tests, should be used to make conclusions about the difference in mean among groups.

### Confidence Intervals

#### 1 Bedroom vs 2 Bedrooms

```{r}
set.seed(20)
B <- 10000
boot_meandiffs <- numeric(B)
n <- nrow(house_sales)

for (i in 1:B) {
boot_ids <- sample(x = 1:n, size = 5000, replace = TRUE)
samp <- house_sales[boot_ids, ]
mean_house_sales_1 <- mean(as.integer(filter(samp, bedrooms == 1)$price))
mean_house_sales_2 <- mean(as.integer(filter(samp, bedrooms == 2)$price))
boot_meandiffs[i] <- mean_house_sales_1 - mean_house_sales_2
}

head(boot_meandiffs)
```

```{r}
CI_boot_12 <- quantile(boot_meandiffs, c(0.025, 0.975))
CI_boot_12
```

```{r}
set.seed(20)
B <- 10000

}

head(boot_meandiffs2)
```

```{r}
CI_boot_13
```

# Model 2 - Not-Necessarily Parallel Lines?

```{r}
model2<-lm(price ~ sqft_living + waterfront + bedrooms+ sqft_living*waterfront, data = house_sales)
summary(model2)
```

## Visualization

```{r}
ggplot(house_sales, aes(x = sqft_living, y = price, color = waterfront)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Least Squares Regression Line for price vs sqft_living")
```
## Diagnostics

### Mean Zero and Homoscedasticity

#### Residuals vs Fitted plot

```{r}
# Residuals vs Fitted
plot(model2, which = 1)
```
Looking at the residuals vs fitted plot, the red line is not centered at 0, it is a upward opening shape with two ends going upward. Most of the data points centered at a small range, that is why the line goes very high at the two ends where there are only few data points.

#### Scale-Location plot

```{r}
# Scale-Location plot
plot(model2, which = 3)
```
Looking at the scale-location plot, it is clear that the variance differs a lot across the dataset. The red line shows a clear up-going trend. This suggests that our data does not fulfill the homoscedasticity assumption.

### Normality

```{r}
model2_withres <- house_sales %>% 
  add_residuals(model2)
qqnorm(model2_withres$resid, main = "Normal Q–Q Plot")
qqline(model2_withres$resid, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```
```{r}
hist(model2_withres$resid, prob = TRUE, breaks = 50, col = "orange",
     main = "Residual Histogram", xlab = "Residuals")
grid <- sort(model2_withres$resid)
lines(grid, dnorm(grid, mean = mean(model2_withres$resid),
                  sd = sd(model2_withres$resid)),
      col = "orange", lwd = 2)
```
From the Q-Q plot, we can see a similar trend as the parallel line model, the points does not align with the line, so normality is not true. Residual histogram shows a very close to normal distribution shape, but there are many outliers that led to no normality.

## Testing & Confidence Interval

### Bootstrap Confidence Interval

```{r}
set.seed(20)
B <- 10000
boot_interactions <- numeric(B)
n <- nrow(house_sales)

for (i in 1:B) {
  boot_ids <- sample(x = 1:n, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  samp <- house_sales[boot_ids, ]

  boot_model2 <- lm(
    price ~ sqft_living * waterfront + bedrooms,
    data = samp
  )

  boot_interactions[i] <- coef(boot_model2)["sqft_living:waterfront1"]
}

head(boot_interactions)
```

```{r}
CI_boot_interaction <- quantile(boot_interactions, c(0.025, 0.975))
CI_boot_interaction
```

### Testing the Interaction

H0: The interaction coefficient equals 0.

HA: The interaction coefficient does not equal 0.

```{r}
reject_H0 <- CI_boot_interaction[1] > 0 | CI_boot_interaction[2] < 0
reject_H0
```

# Other stuff from before - might be useful?

e)  *What does the slope tell you about the relationship between your two variables?* Answer:

There is a positive correlation between sqft_living and price. As sqft_living increases, we expect the price of the property to increase as well.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

f)  Now, add your second continuous predictor variable (predictor 2) to your model, fit the linear regression, and investigate the regression output.

```{r}
linear_2 <- lm(price ~ sqft_living + sqft_lot, data = house_sales)
summary(linear_2)
```

g)  *Compare the slope for your first predictor (predictor 1) between this model and the simple model. Did it change? Why might that happen?* Answer:

In the simple model, the slope of sqft_living used to be 280.624. In this new model with predictor 2 added, the slope is now 282.9. This change might be because now we're taking sqft_lot into consideration as well, where part of the variation in price is now being explained by predictor 2. As a result, for every unit that sqft_living changes, we expect the change in price to be different - meaning that slope changes.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

h)  Now, add in your categorical variable, which you identified previously, to your model. *You should exclude ONE of your continuous predictor variables from this model.* Fit a linear regression model with this information.

```{r}
house_sales$waterfront <- factor(house_sales$waterfront)  # make waterfront categorical

linear_3 <- lm(price ~ sqft_living + waterfront, data = house_sales)
summary(linear_3)
```

i)  Now plot the parallel lines for this model with appropriate labels, using predictions as outlined in the lecture. (Parallel Lines Model)

```{r}
grid_parallel <- expand.grid(
  sqft_living = seq(min(house_sales$sqft_living), max(house_sales$sqft_living), length.out = 50),
  waterfront = levels(house_sales$waterfront)
)

grid_parallel$price_pred <- predict(linear_3, newdata = grid_parallel)
```

We will visualize this by plotting parallel lines by cylinder group.

```{r}
ggplot(house_sales, aes(x = sqft_living, y = price, color = waterfront)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = grid_parallel, aes(y = price_pred, color = waterfront), size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Parallel Lines Model (Additive Effect of waterfront)",
       x = "sqft_living", y = "price") +
  theme_minimal()
```
